chunks: Temperature effects on LiPo performance. The question: How does temperature impact LiPo performance?
Temperature changes how well a lithium cell works. In the cold it gives less power and less usable capacity, because its internal resistance goes up.
Charging it below about 0 degrees Celsius can permanently damage it. In the heat it works well but wears out faster and gets less safe.
So devices measure the temperature and limit charging to a safe window.
Think of honey. At room temperature it pours easily. Put it in the fridge and it flows slowly and resists the spoon. Warm it up and it pours again.
A cold cell is like cold honey: the lithium ions move slowly, so it is harder to pull current out.
The picture breaks in one place: cold honey takes no harm, but charging a cold cell can do lasting damage. A cold cell that is only discharged recovers when it warms up.
The resistance curve is exponential in the cold: each 10 degrees Celsius step below room temperature costs more than the one before. At 0 degrees Celsius you have 2.
5 times the resistance, at minus 20 degrees Celsius roughly 6 times . Real cells vary, so measure yours.
Drag Ea/Rg up to 4500 K (a more temperature-sensitive cell) and the cold-weather penalty at minus 20 degrees Celsius rises to about 15 times .
Internal resistance: the cell's own opposition to current, which grows when cold ("Battery internal resistance").
Voltage sag: the drop in terminal voltage when current flows through that resistance. Lithium plating: lithium turning into metal on the anode during cold or fast charging.
It is permanent and can cause shorts. NTC thermistor: a small sensor whose resistance falls as it warms. The charger reads it to get temperature.
Aging: the slow loss of capacity over time, faster when hot ("LiPo aging and end of life").
Take a 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms internal resistance at 25 degrees Celsius, discharged at 1C, which is 2 amps. The sag is 2 times 0. 05 equals 0. 10 volts.
At 0 degrees Celsius the resistance is roughly 2. 5 times higher, or about 125 milliohms, so the sag is about 0. 25 volts.
The cell hits its cutoff voltage sooner, so you get less capacity out. The same cell would be blocked from charging at that temperature. That is the whole idea.
"Cold makes a LiPo's internal resistance shoot up, roughly 2.
5 times at 0 degrees C and 6 times at minus 20, so you get more voltage sag, an earlier cutoff and less usable capacity, which mostly recovers when it warms up.
Charging in the cold is worse because lithium plates as metal instead of intercalating, which is permanent damage, so chargers block charging below about 0 degrees.
Heat improves performance but speeds up aging and gas formation, and near 60 degrees plus you are eating into safety margin.
So you monitor temperature with an NTC and derate or stop."
